opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it's a good question, and honestly we went back and forth on it quite a bit internally.

The standard approach, if you have an audio codec with multiple codebooks per frame, is to predict those tokens autoregressively. Either you flatten everything, which makes your sequences really long and expensive, or you use some kind of depth transformer or delay pattern to predict the codebooks within a time step. That works, people have shipped good models that way, but it has some annoying properties.

The first is that the residual codebooks aren't independent. When you sample them one after the other, small errors in the early codebooks compound, and you end up spending a lot of compute and engineering on modeling the fine-grained acoustic detail token by token, which is not really where the semantic difficulty is. The backbone model should be thinking about *what* to say and *how* to say it, not about the exact quantization residual of frame 4,312.

With flow matching, you keep the main model autoregressive over time, so you still get streaming and you still get the nice conditioning on everything that came before. But within each time step, you generate the continuous acoustic representation with a small flow head. You're modeling a continuous distribution directly instead of forcing it through a stack of discrete codes. That avoids a lot of the quantization artifacts, and in practice the audio quality, especially things like prosody and voice consistency, was noticeably better for us at comparable model size.

The second reason is latency and efficiency. Flow matching lets you trade off the number of integration steps against quality, and you can get away with very few steps for a small head like that. So compared to sequentially decoding eight or more codebook tokens per frame, it's quite competitive, and it's much easier to parallelize.

And the third thing, which is maybe less obvious, is training stability and simplicity. Flow matching objectives are just very well behaved. You don't have to tune sampling temperatures per codebook, you don't get the weird failure modes where one codebook collapses. It's a cleaner objective.

That said, I don't think autoregressive token prediction is wrong. It's very convenient if you want everything in one unified token space with text, and there are real benefits to that. It's a trade-off. For our use case, where audio quality and streaming latency mattered a lot, the hybrid, autoregressive over time and flow matching within a frame, just gave us the best results.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we debated a lot internally. The thing with autoregressive prediction of audio tokens is that you're committing to a discrete codec, and then at every step you're predicting the next token, and if you're working with a neural codec like EnCodec or something similar, you have multiple codebooks per frame, so you're not even predicting one token per time step, you're predicting eight or sixteen, and you have to deal with that hierarchy somehow — either flatten it, which makes sequences very long, or do some delay pattern trick, which works but adds complexity and latency.

And the quality ceiling is really set by the codec. Whatever the codec throws away, you can never get back. So you end up spending a lot of effort on the tokenizer, and the model itself is always a bit constrained by it.

With flow matching, we work directly in a continuous latent space. You don't have the quantization bottleneck, so the audio fidelity is just better out of the box, especially for things like prosody and the more subtle acoustic details that discrete tokens tend to smooth out. And the training objective is very simple — you're regressing a velocity field, it's a stable loss, there's no mode collapse issues like you'd have with GANs, and you don't have the exposure bias problem you get with autoregressive models where errors compound over long sequences.

The other big thing for us is inference. Autoregressive means one forward pass per token, and for audio at a reasonable frame rate that's a lot of steps for a few seconds of speech. Flow matching lets you generate the whole segment in parallel with a small number of integration steps, so you get much better throughput and you can trade off quality for speed just by changing the number of steps. That's very attractive from a deployment standpoint.

Now, to be fair, autoregressive has advantages too. Streaming is more natural, and the language-model style conditioning is very mature — you can just put text and audio tokens in the same sequence and let the transformer figure it out. So we didn't throw that away completely. The way we think about it is that the autoregressive part handles the high-level structure, the semantic content, the timing, and then flow matching is what actually renders the waveform-level detail. You get the best of both: the sequence modeling where it matters, and a continuous generative model where you need fidelity and speed.

So it's less that we chose one over the other and more that we put each one where it's strongest.

astra-6.text:
The main motivation is that audio is naturally a continuous signal, and predicting discrete audio tokens introduces a bottleneck. You have to decide how to quantize it, how many codebooks to use, and then how to model the dependencies between those tokens. If you predict them sequentially, that can also become expensive in terms of latency.

With flow matching, you can model a continuous distribution and generate a whole chunk of audio jointly. You still have dependencies over time—you can still generate chunks autoregressively—but within a chunk, you don’t need to predict every audio token one after another.

There is a trade-off, because flow matching requires multiple refinement steps. So it’s not automatically faster. But it gives you a useful way to balance compute and audio quality without forcing everything through a discrete token representation.

sol-6.1.text:
The main motivation is that audio is very different from text. With text, you have a relatively compact sequence of discrete tokens. With audio, you have many more time steps, and predicting every audio token autoregressively becomes expensive, especially if you want low latency.

Flow matching lets you model a continuous representation of the audio and generate multiple frames jointly. Instead of committing to one discrete token at a time, you iteratively refine the audio, which is a natural fit for a continuous signal. You also have a useful trade-off between compute and quality through the number of sampling steps.

That doesn’t mean you have to give up causality or streaming. You can still generate audio in chunks, conditioned on what came before. So you preserve the sequential structure where you need it, without making every individual audio token a separate autoregressive step.
